description: Rimlight is a solo team building a 3D simulator for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. Using real NASA terrain data, it shows whether a landing site at the Moon's south pole would have sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth on any date. Mission planners, students and the public can compare sites in seconds.
summary:
Rimlight Navigator is a web app that answers the two questions that decide every lunar landing: will the lander have sunlight for power, and can it see Earth to talk home? Pick any of 20 sites (Apollo, CLPS landers, missions from five countries, NASA Artemis III candidate regions) or type your own coordinates, choose a date, and it shows the Sun and Earth against the real terrain skyline, computed from NASA LOLA laser-altimeter data, with positions validated against NASA JPL Horizons to 0.004°.

It turns that into decisions a planner, teacher or student can read in seconds: a good/workable/poor verdict, countdowns to sunset and Earthset, the best days to land, side-by-side site comparison, a "launch slipped" comparison of two dates, and the seasons month by month. A 3D view and an eye-level mode let anyone stand on the Moon and see why a crater floor gets 0% sunlight while a ridge 20 km away gets 89%.

Searching the whole south pole with NASA's own maps, it also found landing spots with power and Earth contact at the same time 60% of the year, more than any official candidate in the app.
details:
What it does

Rimlight Navigator lets mission planners, educators, and the public compare lunar landing sites and dates quickly. For any site and moment, it shows where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the real local skyline, how long until sunset and Earthset, solar power for upright and flat panels, and whether a direct link to Earth is possible.

It then turns that into decisions:

  • Landing verdict: Good, workable, or poor to land now, using one clear rule: at least 10 days of sunlight before the first sunset, and Earth in view for at least half of the first two weeks.
  • Best days to land: Every day of the month is rated; click one to jump there.
  • Comparisons: Side-by-side comparison of up to four sites, plus "date vs date" comparisons for when a launch slips.
  • Year view: Shows polar seasons (even the sunniest ridge drops from 100% to 62% sunlight in April).
  • Visualizations: 3D terrain, an eye-level "stand on the surface" view, a 360° skyline strip, and a 30-day timeline with playback.
  • Educational features: A 9-scene guided tour, plus "Moon vs Earth" and libration explainers.
  • Sharing and export: Share links and CSV export so science and engineering teams can examine exactly the same scenario.
  • Custom coordinates: Anywhere near the south pole, the real skyline is computed live in the browser from NASA terrain.

How it works

  1. Ephemeris: Sun and Earth positions come from Astronomy Engine, rotated into the Moon's body-fixed frame (IAU model, including libration and topocentric parallax). They agree with NASA JPL Horizons to within 0.004°.
  2. Terrain horizon: For each site, I cast 720 rays out to 300 km through NASA LOLA elevation maps (40 m and 240 m at the pole, 1.9 km globally), including lunar curvature. There's no atmosphere, so no refraction. The Sun or Earth is visible when more than half its disc clears the skyline; power uses the exact visible fraction.
  3. Mission metrics: Sampled every 30–60 minutes over 30 days or a year: sunlit %, Earth-visible %, both at once, longest night, and countdowns refined to the minute.

Validation

  • 160 automated unit tests with 100% coverage of the physics code, including 66 saved NASA JPL Horizons answers.
    • Shackleton–de Gerlache ridge: 88.8% sunlit (literature: approximately 86–89%).
    • Shackleton crater floor: 0% sunlight.
    • Lunar far side: 0% Earth visibility.
    • Best landing windows at the equator: one lunar day (29.6 days) apart.
  • Continuous testing: GitHub Actions runs all tests on every change.

Creativity: Rimlight Picks

I searched every 120 m cell from 85°S to the pole using NASA's LOLA sunlight, Earth-visibility, permanent-shadow, and slope maps, then re-checked the best candidates with our own engine.

Two picks have power and direct Earth contact at the same time for about 60% of the year, versus 49% for the best official candidate in the app, with possible ice (permanent shadow) within 1–5 km.

Clicking a pick jumps to its best 2027 landing date.

Benefits and Impact

When hardware or launch schedules slip, planners can evaluate alternative dates and nearby sites in seconds instead of navigating several expert tools.

Educators and the public get an intuitive way to see why the lunar south pole is so challenging and why past missions like Chandrayaan-3 never woke up after the lunar night.

Tools and Technologies

  • Frontend: JavaScript, Three.js (WebGL 3D), Vite.
  • Astronomy: Astronomy Engine.
  • Testing: Vitest, GitHub Actions.
  • Data processing: Python (NumPy, SciPy, Pillow) for processing NASA data.
  • Hosting: Vercel.
  • Architecture: Static site with no backend, allowing offline functionality.

Factors I Considered

Real topography at the pole, partial Sun discs at grazing angles, lunar curvature, libration, the lack of atmosphere, polar seasons, accessibility for non-specialists (a plain-English verdict, guided tour, and explainers), and honest labelling of limitations (approximate future targets and coarser terrain away from the pole).
